title: Users, Households & Groups
subtitle: The people model in Rec · Admin walkthrough

intro.title: Users, Households & Groups
lines: Groups organize them for pricing & eligibility.
intro.narration: This is how Rec models the people you serve. Every individual user sits inside a household, and this Users directory is where your whole community lives. Groups then organize users for pricing tiers, eligibility rules, and reporting — most commonly, residents versus non-residents. This structure sits behind almost everything a front desk does each day, so getting comfortable here prevents a lot of downstream confusion.

steps.title: Households & profiles
lines: One owner logs in; profiles are members.
Add a family member under Profiles.
steps.narration: Open a household and you'll see everyone in it. One person is the household owner — the account that logs in — and the other profiles are members, like children or family, who don't need their own login. Under Profiles you can add a family member, and from the Actions menu you can edit contact details. One thing to watch: each account needs a unique phone number, so duplicate accounts are the most common cause of a phone-number error.

steps.title: Create & find users
lines: Search by full email or mobile number.
steps.narration: You can create a user yourself with New Account — capturing their name, date of birth for age-restricted programs, phone, and home address for residency. To find someone, your most reliable search is a full email address or mobile number. You can search by name too, but only once that person has registered or transacted with you — and to find a child, search the parent's email.

steps.title: Groups: residents & pricing
lines: One residency group marks your Residents.
steps.narration: Groups are where residency verification and tiered pricing come together. Each organization has a single residency group — here, Niagara Residents — and verified members get resident pricing and early registration automatically. When you create a group you choose its type: Individual, where only specific members qualify; Household, where everyone in the household benefits; or Multi-Participant. Just choose carefully, because the type can't be changed after the group is created.

steps.title: What carries over
lines: Records migrate; history and payments don't.
Businesses and leagues get their own accounts.
We'll map the details in Discovery.
steps.narration: A couple of things worth knowing now. When you move to Rec, household and user records migrate across — but financial transactions, payment information, and past registration history do not, and we'll cover what that means for your team during Discovery. And if you serve businesses, leagues, or outside organizations, those get their own organization accounts, kept separate from individual households.
